subject: english-literature
title: Critical Vocabulary Foundations
welcome_lead: Build the toolkit of terms that turn a comment into a top-band analytical point.
meta_desc: GCSE English Literature — foundational critical vocabulary: motifs, symbolism, juxtaposition and more.
final_note: You can now define and recognise six core critical terms used across the GCSE.

concepts.def: A recurring image, idea or symbol with thematic weight
An object that stands for an abstract idea
Placing two contrasting ideas close together
A hint of an event to come later in the text
A small group standing in for a whole society
A speech revealing a character's private thoughts

walkthroughs.body_html:
A symbol is a single image with a meaning. A motif is a symbol that recurs.

Blood in Macbeth is a motif: it appears as battle gore, guilt on hands, ghosts and Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking. Each return deepens the meaning.

Putting opposites side by side makes both sharper.

Priestley juxtaposes the Birlings' cosy dinner with the news of Eva's death. The contrast forces us to feel the moral gap.

A soliloquy shows what a character truly thinks. The audience knows; other characters don't — that gap is dramatic irony.

Macbeth's 'Is this a dagger which I see before me?' lets us see his madness before Duncan ever does.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a symbol and a motif?
Which technique places two opposites side by side?

numericals.q: How many of the six concepts above are about RECURRING features of a text?
